chapter_title: Introduction to Multi-Area OSPF and Area Types
chapter_summary:
As networks grow in size and complexity, a single-area OSPF design, while simple to implement, quickly becomes inefficient and difficult to manage. A large single OSPF area results in an extensive Link-State Database (LSDB) on every router, requiring more memory and CPU cycles for SPF calculations. Furthermore, any topology change in a large single area triggers a full SPF recalculation across all routers, leading to instability and slow convergence. This is where multi-area OSPF becomes indispensable. Multi-area OSPF introduces a hierarchical structure, dividing the autonomous system into smaller, more manageable areas. This segmentation localizes LSA flooding and SPF calculations, meaning a change in one area only triggers SPF in that specific area and potentially its Area Border Routers (ABRs), significantly improving scalability, stability, and convergence times. The core of any multi-area OSPF design is the backbone area, always designated as Area 0.0.0.0 (or simply Area 0). All other non-backbone areas must connect directly to Area 0. This direct connection ensures a consistent and loop-free path for inter-area routing, as all traffic between non-backbone areas must traverse the backbone.

Beyond the backbone and standard areas, OSPF offers specialized area types designed to further optimize network performance and resource utilization by controlling the propagation of specific Link-State Advertisements (LSAs). A **standard area** is the default OSPF area type, capable of carrying all types of LSAs (Type 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 7 if NSSA). It can host internal routers, ABRs, and Autonomous System Boundary Routers (ASBRs). However, in networks where certain areas don't need to know about external routes (routes learned from other routing protocols) or even inter-area routes, we can implement more restrictive area types.

A **stub area** is designed for spoke sites or areas with limited routing requirements. Stub areas prevent Type 4 and Type 5 LSAs (which describe ASBRs and external routes, respectively) from entering the area. This significantly reduces the LSDB size and SPF calculation overhead for routers within the stub area. Routers in a stub area learn about external destinations via a default route (0.0.0.0/0) injected by the ABR connecting the stub area to the backbone. This default route is represented by a Type 3 LSA. The key restriction is that an ASBR cannot reside within a stub area, as external routes cannot be originated there. To configure a stub area in Junos OS, you'd typically add the `stub` statement under the OSPF area configuration.

Building upon the stub area concept, a **totally stubby area (TSA)** takes the restrictions a step further. In addition to blocking Type 4 and Type 5 LSAs, a TSA also blocks Type 3 LSAs (summary LSAs) that describe inter-area routes. This means routers within a TSA only know about routes within their own area and a single default route (0.0.0.0/0) injected by the ABR. This dramatically shrinks the routing tables and LSDBs of internal routers, making TSAs ideal for very small branch offices or access layer segments. The default route is the only way for routers in a TSA to reach destinations outside their area. To configure a totally stubby area in Junos OS, you would use the `stub no-summaries` statement under the OSPF area configuration on the ABR. It's crucial to remember that all routers within a stub or totally stubby area must agree on the area type, otherwise, OSPF adjacencies will fail.

Finally, we have the **Not-So-Totally Stubby Area (NSSA)**. NSSAs were introduced to address a limitation of stub areas: while stub areas cannot have ASBRs, sometimes it's necessary to connect an external routing domain (e.g., a small branch office running RIP or EIGRP) to an OSPF area that still needs to benefit from some LSA filtering. An NSSA allows an ASBR to reside within it and inject external routes into OSPF. However, instead of generating Type 5 LSAs directly, the ASBR in an NSSA generates Type 7 LSAs. These Type 7 LSAs are then translated by the NSSA ABR into Type 5 LSAs as they are flooded into Area 0. This allows external routes to be advertised out of the NSSA while still preventing Type 4 and Type 5 LSAs from entering the NSSA from Area 0. Like stub areas, NSSAs also receive a default route from their ABR. A further variant is the **NSSA Totally Stubby area**, which combines the NSSA functionality with the filtering of Type 3 LSAs, similar to a totally stubby area. This means it blocks Type 3, 4, and 5 LSAs from entering, but allows Type 7 LSAs to be originated within. To configure an NSSA in Junos OS, you use the `nssa` statement, and for an NSSA totally stubby area, `nssa no-summaries`.

When designing your OSPF network, carefully consider the role of each area. The backbone (Area 0) is mandatory and forms the hub. Standard areas are flexible but can become resource-intensive if too large. Stub and totally stubby areas are excellent for reducing overhead in leaf areas that don't need to advertise or receive a full routing table. NSSAs provide a solution for integrating external routing domains into a stub-like environment. Incorrectly configuring area types, such as placing an ASBR in a stub area or failing to configure all routers in an area with the same area type, are common mistakes that will prevent OSPF from forming adjacencies and propagating routes correctly. Always verify OSPF neighbor states and the LSDB after making area type changes.

screens.title: Introduction to Multi-Area OSPF and Area Types
screens.subtitle: Why OSPF needs hierarchy, and how area types control LSA scope

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn why a flat, single-area OSPF design becomes fragile as networks grow, and how dividing an autonomous system into areas restores scalability and stability. We'll define the backbone area, the standard area, stub and totally stubby areas, and the Not-So-Totally Stubby Area. You will also see the practical limits and operational rules—like the requirement that all non-backbone areas connect to Area 0—and why those rules prevent routing loops and excessive flooding. I'll show concrete Junos configuration examples that match the concepts, and a realistic hands-on scenario where ABRs, an ASBR, and an NSSA interact. Along the way we'll cover common mistakes that break adjacency formation, such as inconsistent area type settings or placing an ASBR inside a stub area. By the end you will understand when to use a stub area at a remote branch, when to use a totally stubby area to shrink routing tables, and when an NSSA is the right compromise to allow local redistribution. As you move forward, think about a specific branch router in your network: should it hold a full routing table, or would a default-only view reduce C P U and memory pressure? That question will guide the choices we make in this chapter.

keyIdea.title: Core Idea
keyIdea.text: Multi-area OSPF introduces a hierarchical structure with Area 0 as the backbone, using area types to limit LSA propagation and reduce LSDB and SPF load on leaf routers.

NSSA

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll build in this chapter

narration.text: These objectives orient practical skills and conceptual understanding you should acquire. First, you'll explain why multi-area OSPF is necessary: a single large area forces every router to keep a huge LSDB and recompute SPF for every topology change. Being able to articulate that performance and stability concern helps you decide when to split an autonomous system into areas. Second, you'll learn to differentiate area types: standard, backbone, stub, totally stubby, and NSSA. That means knowing which LSA types each area allows or blocks and the operational consequences. Third, you'll identify the characteristics and restrictions of each area type, including whether an ASBR is allowed, what LSAs are filtered, and how default routes are injected. Fourth, you'll gain hands-on configuration skills on Junos OS to set area types and common variants. Each objective links concept to practice so you can configure, verify, and explain the outcome of your area design choices in live networks.

screens.title: Why single-area OSPF fails at scale
screens.subtitle: LSDB growth, SPF cost, and instability motivate hierarchy

narration.text: Start here: a single-area OSPF design puts every router in an autonomous system into one shared Link-State Database. That means every router stores all LSAs for the entire AS, increasing memory use and raising C P U cost for SPF calculations. More importantly, any topology change—say a link flapping on one branch—causes SPF recalculation across all routers in that area. In a small network that's manageable. In a large enterprise or campus, repeated global SPF runs cause convergence delays and instability. The remedy is multi-area OSPF: break the AS into smaller areas so LSA flooding and SPF work are contained. When you segment, a link change inside one area typically triggers SPF only for that area and for ABRs that summarize or forward inter-area reachability information. This reduces C P U churn on remote routers. A common misconception is that simply adding areas always fixes performance. In practice, area design must balance management overhead and path visibility; too many small areas complicate summarization and routing policies. Also remember Area 0 is mandatory: all non-backbone areas must connect to Area 0 to assure loop-free inter-area routing. A good rule of thumb is to group devices that share failure domains and similar stability needs into the same area so local changes do not ripple unnecessarily across the network. Reflect on one of your networks and ask: which routers experience the most churn, and would isolating them into their own area improve stability?

keyIdea.title: Problem and solution
keyIdea.text: Large single-area LSDBs and global SPF recalculations cause instability; multi-area OSPF confines flooding and SPF work to improve scalability and convergence.

content.html:
Core Concept Why single-area OSPF fails at scale
The issue: one large LSDB
Every router holds the entire LSDB and runs SPF for every topology change, increasing memory and CPU usage and slowing convergence.
Consequence: widespread SPF events
A single link change forces SPF across all routers in the area, causing delays and potential packet loss during recalculation.
Consequence: larger LSDBs
Routers need more memory and CPU to store and process all LSAs for the whole AS.
Key takeaway
Segmenting into areas localizes changes and protects stability across the network.
Definition and analogy
Think of a single area as one large mailing list where every update is sent to everyone; multi-area OSPF creates smaller lists so only interested routers process local changes.
Concrete example
A campus with 300 routers in one area sees frequent SPF runs when an access switch changes. Splitting access into areas reduces SPF per change to affected areas only.
Common misconception
More areas are not always better; improper design can complicate summarization and increase management overhead.
Check your understanding
Which part of your network experiences the most change, and could isolating it into its own area improve overall stability?

screens.title: The Backbone Area (Area 0)
screens.subtitle: Area 0 is mandatory and provides the inter-area hub

narration.text: Area 0, the backbone, is the mandatory core of any multi-area OSPF design. Its main role is to carry inter-area traffic: all traffic between non-backbone areas must traverse Area 0. This requirement prevents routing loops and keeps inter-area routing predictable. Practically, every non-backbone area must have at least one ABR with a direct adjacency into Area 0. ABRs maintain separate LSDBs per connected area and summarize or forward routes between those LSDBs and the backbone. A common pitfall is creating non-backbone areas that are not physically connected to Area 0, relying instead on virtual links or incorrect summarization; virtual links are an emergency workaround but add operational complexity and should be used sparingly. Another operational detail is that ABRs perform summarization and may inject Type 3 LSAs into connected areas to advertise inter-area routes. Keep Area 0 stable and well-provisioned because instability there affects inter-area reachability across the AS. When designing, place backbone links across reliable transport and avoid hosting transient endpoints directly in Area 0 if they generate frequent topology changes. The Backbone Area (Area 0) means all non-backbone areas must connect to area 0 to ensure loop-free inter-area routing; abrs bridge area lsdbs and inject summaries into connected areas.. In practical terms, area 0 is mandatory and provides the inter-area hub. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Backbone rule
keyIdea.text: All non-backbone areas must connect to Area 0 to ensure loop-free inter-area routing; ABRs bridge area LSDBs and inject summaries into connected areas.

content.html:
Definition Backbone Area (Area 0)
Role and requirement
Area 0 is the central hub for inter-area routing. All non-backbone areas must connect to it to ensure consistent inter-area paths and avoid loops.
ABR responsibilities
Maintain separate LSDBs per area, advertise inter-area routes as Type 3 LSAs, and translate Type 7 to Type 5 for NSSAs when needed.
Operational advice
Keep the backbone on stable links. Avoid placing highly dynamic endpoints directly in Area 0 that would force inter-area instability.
Analogy and example
Treat Area 0 like a central highway system. Local roads (non-backbone areas) must connect to the highway to reach other local roads, and the highway should be reliable and well-maintained.
Concrete example
An ABR connecting Area 1 and Area 2 to Area 0 advertises summarized inter-area routes as Type 3 LSAs into each area so routers can reach remote prefixes.
Common mistake
Non-backbone areas not connected to Area 0, or inconsistent area type settings across routers, will break adjacencies or inter-area routing.

screens.title: Standard areas and LSA types
screens.subtitle: What a standard area carries and when to use it

narration.text: A standard OSPF area is the default area type and carries the full set of LSAs relevant to its internal and external reachability. That includes Type 1 and Type 2 LSAs for intra-area routers and networks, Type 3 and Type 4 LSAs for inter-area summaries, and Type 5 LSAs for external routes redistributed into OSPF. If an area is also an NSSA, it may carry Type 7 LSAs originating from an internal ASBR. Standard areas are flexible: they can host internal routers, ABRs, and ASBRs. The flexibility, however, comes with cost—because standard areas accept Type 5 LSAs, routers must store and possibly process external LSAs from other routing domains, which increases LSDB size. Use a standard area where routers need full visibility of external or inter-area routes, such as a data center or core site. A common misconception is that standard areas are always the simplest answer; they are simple to configure but may not be appropriate for leaf sites where resource constraints or policy require limiting external routes. When planning, choose standard areas for sections of the network requiring full routing information and prefer stub/TSA/NSSA variants at remote branches that can operate with a default route.

keyIdea.title: Standard area
keyIdea.text: Standard areas carry Types 1–5 LSAs and are suitable where full route visibility is required, but they can increase LSDB and SPF load.

content.html:
Definition Standard Area
What a standard area carries
  • Type 1, 2: intra-area router and network LSAs.
  • Type 3, 4: inter-area summaries from ABRs.
  • Type 5: external LSAs from ASBRs (and Type 7 translated when NSSA ABR converts them).
When to use
Deploy standard areas at sites that require full routing visibility, like cores or service aggregation points.
Analogy and example
A standard area is like a full-membership network where everyone receives all updates, suitable where nodes need complete information.
Example
A data center area that hosts ASBRs will likely be standard to accept external Type 5 LSAs and advertise them into the AS.
Misconception
Assuming 'default area' equals 'best for all' is incorrect; leaf routers may benefit from restricted LSA types to conserve resources.

screens.title: Stub Areas — behavior and configuration
screens.subtitle: Block Type 4 and Type 5 LSAs; rely on a default route from the ABR

narration.text: A stub area is a restricted OSPF area intended for leaf or spoke sites with limited routing needs. The defining behavior of a stub area is that it blocks Type 4 and Type 5 LSAs, which describe ASBR summaries and external routes. Because external LSA types are suppressed, routers inside a stub area do not learn external or ASBR-specific routes directly. Instead, the ABR injects a default route, represented as a Type 3 LSA, so internal routers can reach external destinations via the ABR. This significantly reduces LSDB size and the SPF workload on spoke routers. Operationally, an ASBR cannot exist within a stub area—attempting to place one there contradicts the area’s intent and will prevent correct external route origination. On Junos OS you configure a stub area by adding the stub statement under the OSPF area configuration on the ABR and all area routers must agree on the area type. A common mistake is mixing area types in the same area across routers, which breaks adjacency formation. Stub areas are ideal when branch routers need only local prefixes plus internet access via a default route, not full external route visibility.

keyIdea.title: Stub area rule
keyIdea.text: Stub areas block Type 4 and Type 5 LSAs and rely on a default route from the ABR; ASBRs cannot be placed inside a stub.

content.html:
Core Concept Stub Area
Behavior
Blocks Type 4 and Type 5 LSAs. Routers inside learn a default route from the ABR and keep only local and default routes.
Configuration note
On Junos, add the 'stub' statement under the OSPF area on the ABR. All routers in the area must use the same area type.
Common error
Placing an ASBR in a stub area or mismatched area type settings prevents adjacency and external route propagation.
Example and takeaway
Use a stub area for a remote branch that only needs local prefixes and internet access via a default route injected by the ABR.
Concrete example
R3 in Area 0.0.0.2 configured as stub will not see Type 5 LSAs and will learn 0.0.0.0/0 from its ABR.
Check
Verify absence of Type 4/5 LSAs in the LSDB and the presence of a default route injected by the ABR.

screens.title: Totally Stubby Areas (TSA)
screens.subtitle: Block Type 3, 4, and 5 — only a default is learned

narration.text: A Totally Stubby Area extends the stub area concept by blocking Type 3 LSAs in addition to Type 4 and Type 5 LSAs. The result is that routers inside a TSA only know about their local area routes and a single default route injected by the ABR. This produces the smallest LSDB and routing table for leaf routers and is ideal for very small branch offices or access-layer segments with limited routing needs. The ABR must be configured to inject the default route and disable summaries, typically with 'stub no-summaries' on Junos. All routers inside the TSA must agree on the area type or adjacency formation will fail. Be mindful that because Type 3 summaries are blocked, routers in a TSA have no visibility into inter-area prefixes except via the default route, so policy-based routing or split-horizon requirements may be affected. A common misconception is that TSAs are appropriate everywhere for savings; in reality they trade away route granularity and prevent local load-based decisions for remote prefixes. Use TSAs when branch routers have no need to select among multiple inter-area paths and can rely on the ABR default for all non-local destinations.

keyIdea.title: TSA behavior
keyIdea.text: Totally Stubby Areas block Type 3, 4, and 5 LSAs so internal routers keep only local routes and a default route, minimizing LSDB and routing table size.

content.html:
Core Concept Totally Stubby Area
What is blocked
  • Type 3 LSAs (inter-area summaries) are blocked.
  • Type 4 and Type 5 LSAs are also blocked like a stub area.
  • The ABR advertises only a default route (no summaries).
Configuration
On Junos, configure the ABR area with 'stub no-summaries' to create a TSA.
Use case and caution
TSA is ideal for tiny branches where only a default route is acceptable. Beware that blocking Type 3 removes inter-area route granularity and may prevent optimal path selection for remote prefixes.
Example
A branch with constrained CPU and memory can be TSA to conserve resources and rely solely on the ABR's default route for external reachability.
Misconception
Assuming TSA preserves inter-area routing detail is false; it intentionally removes that detail to minimize routing state.

screens.title: NSSA and NSSA Totally Stubby
screens.subtitle: Allow local redistribution while still limiting external LSAs

narration.text: The Not-So-Totally Stubby Area, or NSSA, solves a practical limitation of stub areas: sometimes a leaf area needs to host an ASBR to redistribute external routes while still benefiting from filtering of other external LSAs. In an NSSA, an ASBR can originate external routes as Type 7 LSAs. These Type 7 LSAs are flooded within the NSSA and are translated by the NSSA ABR into Type 5 LSAs when advertised into Area 0. NSSAs still block Type 4 and Type 5 LSAs from entering the area from other parts of the AS, so the internal view remains constrained. The ABR also injects a default route into the NSSA so internal routers can reach non-local destinations. There is also an NSSA Totally Stubby variant that combines NSSA capabilities with the suppression of Type 3 summaries, blocking Type 3, 4, and 5 LSAs while still allowing Type 7 origination. In Junos OS you configure nssa or nssa no-summaries depending on whether you want the totally stubby behavior. A misconception to avoid is assuming Type 7 LSAs behave identically to Type 5; they must be translated by the ABR to become Type 5 for the rest of the AS to see them. Verify Type 7 presence on the ASBR's LSDB and translation at the ABR when testing NSSA setups.

keyIdea.title: NSSA summary
keyIdea.text: NSSAs allow an ASBR inside a restricted area by using Type 7 LSAs locally, which ABRs translate to Type 5 for the backbone while still blocking other external LSAs.

content.html:
Core Concept NSSA and NSSA Totally Stubby
How NSSA works
ASBRs inside an NSSA generate Type 7 LSAs for redistributed routes; the NSSA ABR translates those Type 7 LSAs into Type 5 before flooding into Area 0.
NSSA Totally Stubby
Combines NSSA origination with 'no-summaries' so Type 3, 4, and 5 are blocked while Type 7 is allowed.
Practical use
Use NSSA when a branch must redistribute a small external domain but still needs LSDB filtering for scale.
Verification and gotchas
Check for Type 7 LSAs on the ASBR and confirm translation to Type 5 at the ABR. Ensure area type consistency to avoid adjacency problems.
Configuration hint
On Junos, use 'nssa' for NSSA and 'nssa no-summaries' for NSSA totally stubby behavior on the ABR and area routers.
Misconception
Assuming Type 7 LSAs automatically propagate like Type 5 across the AS is false; translation by the ABR is required.

screens.title: ABR and ASBR roles in multi-area OSPF
screens.subtitle: How border routers manage LSDBs, summaries, and translations

narration.text: Border routers are the operational glue of a multi-area OSPF design. An Area Border Router, or ABR, connects one or more non-backbone areas to Area 0 and maintains separate LSDBs for each area it touches. ABRs translate internal LSAs into Type 3 summaries for other areas and, in the case of NSSAs, translate Type 7 LSAs into Type 5 when propagating external routes into the backbone. An Autonomous System Boundary Router, or ASBR, is the device that redistributes routes from an external domain into OSPF. In a standard area, an ASBR originates Type 5 LSAs. In an NSSA, the ASBR originates Type 7 LSAs instead. Understanding these roles helps you reason about where SPF is calculated and where LSA types change meaning. A key operational point: ABRs only forward necessary LSAs between LSDBs and can inject default routes into stub or TSA areas. When designing, place ABRs where summarization and control over external visibility are required. A common mistake is to place an ASBR inside a stub area; this violates area rules and prevents redistributing external routes correctly. Always verify the LSDB on ABRs and ASBRs to confirm expected behavior.

keyIdea.title: Border routers
keyIdea.text: ABRs connect areas and summarize or translate LSAs; ASBRs introduce external routes into OSPF as Type 5 or Type 7 depending on area type.

content.html:
Process Flow ABR and ASBR roles
ABR responsibilities
  • Maintain separate LSDBs for each connected area.
  • Advertise inter-area routes as Type 3 LSAs into connected areas.
  • Translate Type 7 LSAs to Type 5 when exporting NSSA-originated externals to Area 0.
Operational tip
Review LSDBs on ABRs to confirm summarization and translation behavior after configuration changes.
ASBR responsibilities
The ASBR injects external routes into OSPF. In standard areas it originates Type 5 LSAs; in NSSAs it originates Type 7 LSAs.
Concrete example
R5 in Area 0.0.0.3 is an ASBR in the lab scenario and redistributes a static route as Type 7 LSA in the NSSA.
Misconception
Assuming ABRs simply proxy LSAs without maintaining per-area LSDBs is incorrect; ABRs maintain distinct databases and perform translation and summarization actions.

You should type these commands on the appropriate routers and commit, then verify adjacency and LSDB behavior. Remember that every router inside a stub or NSSA area must share the same area type or adjacencies will fail. The code block below reproduces the area-focused configuration. After applying these statements, use the verification steps we cover later to confirm Type 7 LSAs on the ASBR and their translation at the ABR. In practical terms, translate the design into area statements and nssa/stub options. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. keyIdea.title: Config focus

Code Walkthrough Junos OSPF area snippets
Selected snippets

set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface lo0.0
set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/1.0

set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.1 interface ge-0/0/2.0
set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.1 type standard

set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.2 interface ge-0/0/3.0
set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.2 stub


<!-- R4: ABR for Area 0 and Area 3 (NSSA) -->

set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface lo0.0

set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.3 interface ge-0/0/1.0
set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.3 nssa

set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.3 interface lo0.0

set routing-options static route 192.168.100.0/24 next-hop 10.0.0.254
set policy-options policy-statement REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC term 1 from protocol static
set policy-options policy-statement REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC term 1 then accept
set protocols ospf export REDISTRIBUTE_STATIC
Practical notes
  • Replace interface names and next-hop addresses to match your lab topology.
  • Apply area statements consistently across all routers in an area to avoid adjacency failures.
  • Use policy export on the ASBR to control which static routes are redistributed into OSPF.
Key takeaway

screens.title: Verification steps after area changes
screens.subtitle: Commands and observable outcomes to confirm correct behavior

narration.text: After configuring area types, verification is essential. Start by checking OSPF neighbor states on every router with the show ospf neighbor command to ensure adjacencies have formed. Next, inspect the LSDB on representative routers: for a stub area router, use show ospf database extensive and confirm that Type 4 and Type 5 LSAs are absent; for an NSSA ASBR, look for Type 7 LSAs in its LSDB. On the NSSA ABR, verify translation by confirming Type 5 LSAs representing the redistributed prefixes appear in the backbone LSDB. Finally, check the routing table on internal routers: routers in stub or TSA should show a single default route (0.0.0.0/0) learned via OSPF, while routers in standard areas will have inter-area and external routes present. A common troubleshooting step is to re-check area type consistency if adjacencies fail or expected LSAs are missing. Also verify route redistribution policies on ASBRs to ensure only the intended prefixes are exported. These verification steps close the loop between configuration and operational behavior and should be part of any area type change workflow. narration.text: This hands-on activity ties the chapter together. The scenario asks you to configure R1 as an ABR connecting Area 0 to Area 1 (standard) and Area 2 (stub); R2 as an internal router in Area 1; R3 as an internal router in Area 2 (stub); R4 as an ABR connecting Area 0 to Area 3 (NSSA); and R5 as an ASBR within Area 3 redistributing a static route. Begin by applying the provided area statements on each router and commit the configuration. On R5, configure the static route and a policy-statement to export it into OSPF so it will appear as a Type 7 LSA inside the NSSA. After the configuration commits, verify adjacencies with show ospf neighbor. On R3 confirm that Type 4 and Type 5 LSAs are absent and that a default route exists. On R5 verify Type 7 LSAs exist for the redistributed 192.168.100.0/24 prefix, and on R1 or R4 verify the ABR has translated the Type 7 into a Type 5 in Area 0. screens.title: Common mistakes and best practices
screens.subtitle: Avoiding misconfigurations and designing for stability

narration.text: When implementing multi-area OSPF, a few recurring mistakes cause the majority of issues. The first is inconsistent area type configuration: all routers in an area must agree on whether it is stub, totally stubby, or NSSA; mismatch prevents adjacency and breaks reachability. Second, placing an ASBR inside a stub or TSA is invalid and will prevent proper external LSA origination—ASBRs belong in standard or NSSA areas depending on desired behavior. Third, overusing virtual links to connect non-backbone areas to Area 0 can mask poor topology design and introduce fragility; prefer physical or routed backbone connectivity where possible. Best practices include keeping Area 0 stable and using ABRs for summarization, deploying stub or TSA at leaf sites where only a default route is needed, and using NSSA for branches that must redistribute small external domains. Always verify neighbor states and the LSDB after changes. Lastly, document area boundaries and ABR roles so future engineers understand where summarization, translation, and redistribution occur. These habits reduce human error and keep multi-area OSPF predictable and manageable. Comparison Common mistakes vs Best practices
Common mistakes
  • Inconsistent area type settings across routers in the same area.
  • Placing ASBRs inside a stub or TSA.
  • Overreliance on virtual links to bypass proper backbone connectivity.
Best practices
  • Keep Area 0 stable and well-connected; use ABRs for summarization and translation.
  • Use stub/TSA at branches that only need a default route to reduce LSDB size.
  • Use NSSA when local redistribution is required while still limiting external LSA exposure.
Takeaway
Design with consistency and operational verification in mind: configure, verify, document.

narration.text: These concept cards summarize the fundamentals you should carry forward. Multi-Area OSPF divides the autonomous system into smaller areas so LSA flooding and SPF calculations are localized, improving scalability and convergence. Area 0 is the mandatory backbone and must connect all non-backbone areas to provide loop-free inter-area routing. The standard area is the default type and carries all LSA types, making it suitable when full route visibility is required but costly in terms of LSDB size. content.html:
What to Remember
Multi-Area OSPF
Divide an AS into areas to localize LSA flooding and SPF work for better scalability and convergence.
Backbone Area (Area 0)
All non-backbone areas must connect to Area 0 to ensure loop-free inter-area routing and consistent path selection.
Standard Area
Default area type that carries LSAs 1–5 and optionally 7, useful for cores but costlier for LSDB size.
Summary Takeaway

Design areas to contain change and assign area types according to each site's need for external and inter-area visibility.

narration.text: These final cards capture area-type specifics and operational roles you will use daily. A stub area blocks Type 4 and Type 5 LSAs and receives a default route from the ABR, making it suitable for simple spokes. A Totally Stubby Area blocks Type 3 as well, further reducing LSDB size so branch routers only keep local routes plus a default; use it where only a default is needed. The NSSA allows an ASBR inside a restricted area by originating Type 7 LSAs, which ABRs translate to Type 5 when advertising into the backbone. Always verify LSDB contents and routing tables after changes and ensure area-type consistency to avoid common adjacency and propagation errors. Key Concepts — Part 2 means use stub/tsa/nssa to control lsa propagation and place asbrs and abrs according to area rules; always verify lsdbs and routes after changes.. keyIdea.title: Operational rules
keyIdea.text: Use stub/TSA/NSSA to control LSA propagation and place ASBRs and ABRs according to area rules; always verify LSDBs and routes after changes.

content.html:
What to Remember
Stub Area
Blocks Type 4 and 5 LSAs; receives a Type 3 default route from the ABR. No ASBR allowed inside.
Totally Stubby Area
Blocks Type 3, 4, and 5 LSAs; routers only learn local prefixes and a single default route injected by the ABR.
NSSA
Allows an ASBR to originate Type 7 LSAs. The ABR translates Type 7 to Type 5 for the backbone while blocking external LSAs from entering the NSSA.
Final takeaway

Choose the least-permissive area type that meets reachability needs, verify LSDBs and routing tables, and document ABR/ASBR responsibilities to maintain predictable OSPF behavior.
